statement: In 113 people (the review's table sums to 116) with eye problems after using poppers described in 32 published case reports, case series and conference abstracts (2004 to 2021, pooled in a systematic review searched to November 2021; 108 men, average age 40, more than half reported from the UK), the reports describe a consistent picture: both eyes affected in 67 of 69 with details, with reduced or blurred central vision, flashes and other visual disturbances, or a central blind spot; a yellow spot at the centre of the retina on examination in 53 of 72, and disruption of the layer of light-sensing cells at the centre of the retina on scans in 89 of 111. Use ranged from a single occasion to more than 20 years, and the product was not named for 100 of 113. In those followed up, scans had improved or returned to normal in 46 of 75 (61%), and average sharpness of vision improved from 0.24 to 0.11 logMAR (from about 6/9.5 to about 6/7.5) in 79 eyes of 40 people. With no comparison group and selective follow-up, the reports cannot show how often poppers harm the eyes, which products or patterns of use carry the risk, or how the many people not followed up fared. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: Eye doctors in many countries have described people whose central vision became blurry or dim after using poppers, sometimes after a single use, with damage to the light-sensing cells at the centre of the eye; in most of those checked again, the damage got better. These are reports of people who saw an eye doctor, so they cannot tell how often this happens or with which poppers.
population: People with eye problems after recreational poppers use described in 32 published reports (113 patients), 2004 to 2021
exposure: Inhaled poppers (alkyl nitrites; compound named for 13 of 113)
outcome: Symptoms and eye findings at presentation (poppers maculopathy) and change in vision and retinal scans at follow-up
magnitude: Both eyes 67 of 69 (97.1%); complaints (81 in 56 people): acuity changes 36 (44.4%), visual disturbances 29 (35.7%), central scotoma 15 (18.5%); yellow foveal spot 53 of 72 (73.6%); ellipsoid-layer disturbance on OCT 89 of 111 (80.1%); OCT improved or resolved 46 of 75 (61.3%); mean acuity 0.24 to 0.11 logMAR in 79 eyes of 40 people (Wilcoxon Z = −5.800, p < 0.001, eyes treated as independent); 9 of 69 best eyes (13%) at 0.4 logMAR or worse at presentation, 2 followed up, unchanged.

statement: In young people in the United States in the 1960s, sudden deaths right after sniffing volatile hydrocarbons (solvents and aerosol sprays), without suffocation in a plastic bag, were described in a series of 110 deaths gathered by a nationwide survey in 1969 whose methods are not described (Bass, 1970). Those who died were aged 11 to 23, and 37 were known to have sniffed before, occasionally or habitually; the products were mostly aerosol propellants (fluorocarbons; 59 deaths) and the cleaning solvent 1,1,1-trichloroethane (29), then toluene (8), benzene (7) and gasoline (4) (editors' sums of the paper's map); the report lists no alkyl nitrite (poppers). Where an autopsy is described, it found no anatomical cause of death; volatile hydrocarbons were found in the organs in 44 deaths (how many were tested is not given), so a positive toxicological result is not reported for most of the series; how the remaining cases were classified is not stated. In six eyewitness accounts the person suddenly ran, screamed or became agitated, or called out that his heart was stopping, just before collapsing; eight people dashed a few hundred feet and then collapsed; and an activity or stress, such as being surprised by parents or police, running from police, wrestling or riding a bicycle, was listed for 18 deaths. Family or friends hid the sniffing in 8 deaths. Products considered of low toxicity on the basis of human and animal experiments were among those involved. The author proposed that the hydrocarbons make the heart prone to a sudden fatal rhythm, intensified by raised carbon dioxide or by adrenaline from fright or exertion, drawing on cat and anaesthesia studies; no heart rhythm was recorded in any death, and he wrote that it is difficult to say what caused the terminal event accompanied by panic. With no count of how many people sniffed, the series cannot say how often sniffing ends in sudden death or whether this was becoming more common (the abstract's 'sharp rise' in incidence has no rate behind it), and without sniffing episodes that did not end in death to compare with, it cannot show that fright or exertion raises the risk. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In the United States in the 1960s, 110 young people aged 11 to 23 died suddenly right after sniffing solvents or aerosol sprays, mostly spray propellants or a cleaning solvent; the report did not list poppers. Where an autopsy was described, it found no other cause of death, and several people suddenly ran or panicked just before they collapsed. The author proposed that the chemicals upset the heart's rhythm, with stress, effort or a build-up of carbon dioxide adding to this. No heart trace was recorded; this was a proposed explanation from other studies. The survey counted deaths, not how many people sniffed, so it cannot say how often this happens.
population: 110 young people (aged 11 to 23) in the United States who died suddenly after sniffing volatile hydrocarbons in the 1960s (1962 to 1 April 1969), found through a nationwide survey in 1969 that followed a telephone survey of East Coast medical examiner offices
exposure: Sniffing volatile hydrocarbons: aerosol fluorocarbon propellants, 1,1,1-trichloroethane, toluene, benzene, gasoline (classification methods unstated; positive organ toxicology reported in 44 deaths, with the number tested unknown); deaths with plastic-bag suffocation excluded
outcome: Sudden death: the circumstances just before collapse, autopsy and toxicology findings
magnitude: Bass (1970): 110 deaths; by chemical (editors' sums of Figure 2): aerosol fluorocarbon propellants 59, 1,1,1-trichloroethane 29, toluene 8, benzene 7, gasoline 4, toluene with trichloroethane 2, unidentified 1; by region West 57, Central 18, East 35; ages 11 to 23; history of occasional or habitual sniffing 37; activity or stress listed for 18 (16 in 100, editors' calculation, a lower bound of recorded circumstances, not a frequency); sudden dash before collapse in 8 witnessed deaths; volatile hydrocarbons found at toxicology in 44 (number tested not given), quantified in 12; sniffing concealed by family or friends in 8. No rate can be computed.

risk_of_bias.note: Card sc_bass_1970, JBI checklist, high: deaths gathered by an undescribed survey, with no case definition or attribution criteria; toxicology reported positive in 44 of 110 with the number tested unknown; circumstances recorded for few deaths; no comparison group.

indirectness.note: Worded for the series' place, period and products; it is not applied to poppers (alkyl nitrites), which the report does not list.

imprecision.note: No estimate is given; counts only.

grade.reasoning: A case series without a comparison starts low; rated down for risk of bias: very low. The claim describes the deaths that were recorded, as the paper allows; it gives no rate, trend or risk factor, and the heart-rhythm explanation is reported as the author's proposal from animal and anaesthesia studies, not as a finding. The counts are a minimum: the survey's completeness is unknown, and concealment means that some deaths after sniffing were probably not recognized. The claim covers solvents and aerosol sprays only. Later death series (for example Darke et al., 2023, on the reading list) were not read. Status single study.

statement: In people diagnosed with eye damage after using poppers (113 people in 32 published reports, 2004 to 2021, pooled in a systematic review), evidence is insufficient to say whether stopping poppers, or taking lutein supplements, compared with continuing or not taking them, helps vision recover: treatment was documented for 45 people, of whom 42 were advised to stop (3 of them also given lutein) and 2 were given lutein alone; whether people really stopped was recorded for 27 (19 had); there was no comparison group, and the review states that the effect of treatment or of stopping on vision could not be analysed. Scans improved in most of those followed up (46 of 75), but this cannot be tied to stopping: of the two people followed longest, one who reportedly kept using had unchanged vision and one whose stopping was not recorded improved, and some earlier series saw no improvement in the first months despite stopping. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: Most people with this eye damage were told to stop using poppers, and a few were given lutein, a supplement, but nobody compared them with people who did not stop, so we do not know whether stopping or lutein helps the eyes recover. Many got better over time either way, as far as the reports show.
population: People diagnosed with eye damage after poppers use (113 published cases, 2004 to 2021)
exposure: Stopping poppers use, or oral lutein
comparator: Continuing use, or no lutein (no comparison group in the reports)
outcome: Recovery of vision and of retinal findings
magnitude: No comparative data. Stopping advised for 42 of the 45 with treatment documented; lutein for 5 (3 with stopping, 2 alone); compliance recorded for 27 (19 compliant); OCT improved or resolved in 46 of 75 followed up, without data by stopping.
